stories.headline: OpenCode discloses a breach tied to a 'large scale distillation attack' and tells affected users to rotate their provider keys
stories.why_read: AI Top Story: you retweeted it twice and bookmarked it, and it's one of the biggest threads on Hacker News this weekend. If you wire your own API keys into an AI coding tool, this one is about you.
body: The open-source coding agent OpenCode said Saturday that it had a security breach the night before, related to what it called a large scale distillation attack. It says 1.4% of OpenCode Console users were affected, all of them people who had linked external model providers, and that every affected user got an email Saturday morning. If you didn't get one, OpenCode says you weren't impacted. The company added that the incident is still ongoing and that it is working with Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google to remediate.

The security crowd moved faster than the official post. Matt Johansen wrote 'Confirmed. OpenCode hacked. Keys stolen,' and said customers were being told to revoke, and NetworkChuck's post that you retweeted boiled it down to 'Change your keys!' The Hacker News thread passed 870 points. OpenCode hasn't explained exactly how the distillation attack and the leaked keys connect, but the practical step is the same either way: rotate any provider keys you've pasted into a third-party agent console.

stories.headline: Tesla's Austin Robotaxi fleet passes 400 cars, and Musk says Optimus and Cybercab will be most of Tesla's value
stories.why_read: Top Story: you retweeted the fleet count last night, and it's happening on the streets around you. Pair it with Musk's own framing and you get the clearest picture yet of where Tesla thinks its money is.
body: Tesla tracker @TSLAFanMtl, whose post you retweeted, counts just over 400 vehicles in Tesla's Austin Robotaxi fleet, with roughly 360 of them, about 90%, appearing active. Service runs 6 AM to midnight, 18 hours a day, which works out to about 6,500 car-hours daily. His estimate: to cover all of Austin's rideshare demand at today's traditional rideshare pricing, Tesla would need only about 3,000 robotaxis running around the clock, or about 4,445 at 90% utilization on the current 18-hour schedule. He says Austin is the market to watch for how competitors respond and how robotaxi economics play out elsewhere.

The same day, X News reports, Musk posted that only superintelligence, robots, solar power, and space travel scale to enormous economic size, with Tesla leading in the first two, and said Optimus and Cybercab will make up the vast majority of Tesla's value. He called the next-generation Roadster a cool side project rather than a core focus. Observers largely agreed that autonomy and robotics, not car sales, hold Tesla's upside, while flagging competition from China.

stories.headline: Anthropic's own data: junior technical hires fell from 27% to 9% as agent hours grew to six times human hours
stories.why_read: New on Hacker News this morning, and it reads like a field report from the future of your org. Every platform leader managing thousands of engineers should see these numbers.
body: Anthropic economists Nathan Wilmers, Regina Catipon, Maxim Massenkoff, and Peter McCrory studied the company itself, using internal data on employment, AI use, output, surveys, calendars, and hiring records plus 17 employee interviews. The share of junior-level employees in technical departments slipped from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the share of junior technical hires fell faster, from 27% to 9%. By August, interactive AI agent hours outnumbered employees' hours six to one, and output per person rose as each employee adopted new tools. At five years old, Anthropic takes in two to four times as much revenue per employee as Meta and Google did at the same stage of their growth.

The bottleneck has moved to human attention: even for non-technical staff, reading everything their Claude agents produce would take half the work week, so people shift to 'meta-work' like building visibility tools and monitoring agent pipelines. One engineer described facing 'an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention.' Hiring managers now weigh autonomy and judgment over domain expertise, and Anthropic says it has set up an early warning system for jobs at risk and prioritized internal redeployment.

stories.headline: DeepSeek launches its own Search and Fetch APIs for agents at $0.75 per 1,000 successful requests
stories.why_read: The number one story on Hacker News right now. Right after V4.1 Flash, DeepSeek is selling the web-access layer that every agent stack needs, at a price that undercuts most search APIs.
body: DeepSeek now offers two raw JSON endpoints powered by its in-house search engine: Search returns structured results for a query, and Fetch retrieves a single page and returns it as Markdown. Both use the same bearer key as the DeepSeek API. Search accepts familiar operators such as site:, -site:, lang:, after:, and before:, returns up to 50 results per call, and each result carries a relevance score, a short UI snippet, and a longer 600 to 800 character summary written to be read by a model.

Billing is per successful request, not per token or per result: $0.75 per 1,000 for each API. Failed requests, empty results, and timeouts aren't billed. The docs note that server-side tool calls made through DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code, or Codex already hit these APIs and are free for now, with per-request billing set to begin in November.

stories.headline: vLLM and Nvidia push Kimi K3 to 423 tokens per second per user on GB300s
stories.why_read: Inference engineering at its most concrete: same model, same GPUs, much faster, all from software. Exactly your Nvidia and open-model beat.
body: X News reports the vLLM project has integrated specialized decode kernels written with Nvidia's CuTe DSL that fuse attention, mixture-of-experts, and communication work. The result is up to 423 tokens per second per user for Kimi K3 on 16 GB300 GPUs, and 842 tokens per second at batch size 1 with speculative decoding, along with 1.5 to 2 times higher throughput on agentic workloads.

The backend is opt-in and targets tensor parallelism across 8 or 16 GPUs. The community praised the roughly 12,000-line optimization and the AI-assisted way it was built, while arguing over whether 'megakernel' is the right label and how fair the baseline comparisons are.

stories.headline: Solar out-generated nuclear worldwide for the first time in 2025, while nuclear capacity barely moved
stories.why_read: Energy Tech from your pinned post, with 600-plus points and nearly 400 comments on Hacker News. The growth curves here are almost comically lopsided.
body: The World Nuclear Industry Status Report 2026, overseen by consultant Mycle Schneider, finds that wind passed nuclear on a monthly basis in March 2025 and solar did so in April, the first time global monthly solar generation beat nuclear. From March 2025 through June 2026, solar or wind alone out-generated nuclear every month. Over 2025, global solar capacity grew by 510 GW to 2,383 GW and wind added a record 159 GW, while installed nuclear capacity rose just 1.5 GW to 399.5 GW. Solar generation jumped about 30% for the year, enough to surpass nuclear's annual output.

pv magazine notes the report's solar numbers are conservative: IEA PVPS puts 2025 PV additions near 690 GW, about 180 GW more. Schneider was blunt about the nuclear startups, pointing to Holtec pausing its IPO days before listing and Fermi losing about 80% of its stock value since its October 2025 debut, because they have 'little or nothing to show on the ground.'

stories.headline: Google's Willow chip demonstrates magic state cultivation, producing T-states at 99.99% logical fidelity
stories.why_read: Physics right at the top of your pinned post. This tackles one of the most stubborn bottlenecks between today's quantum chips and useful error-corrected algorithms.
body: X News reports Google Quantum AI researchers demonstrated magic state cultivation on real hardware, published in Science on October 15. Using about 54 qubits on the Willow chip, the team produced T-states with 99.99% logical fidelity and cut errors about 40 times compared with earlier methods. The process filters aggressively: only about 8% of attempts pass its checks.

Magic states are the ingredient error-corrected machines need for the gates that make quantum algorithms more powerful than classical ones, and producing them cheaply has been a major bottleneck. Crypto watchers flagged long-term risks to Bitcoin's security, though analysts say scaling to anything threatening remains far off.

stories.headline: The AI build-out runs on debt: NYT compares CoreWeave to WeWork as Anthropic lines up $60 billion for TPUs
stories.why_read: You retweeted the CoreWeave piece. Put it next to Anthropic's chip financing and you get the money side of the inference boom you follow so closely.
body: Carl Quintanilla, whose post you retweeted, highlighted a New York Times line on AI debt: 'CoreWeave's business model defies easy description. Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts to that of the troubled office-space provider WeWork.' The Times piece looks at the borrowing behind the AI infrastructure boom across CoreWeave, Oracle, and SoftBank.

Anthropic is part of the same story. X News reports it is tapping a $60 billion debt package called Project North Star, through Blackstone-managed funds, to buy 1.5 gigawatts of Google's TPUs, with Blackstone committing $9 billion in junior debt backed by Anthropic's five-year lease payments at yields above 10%. Separately, X News reports Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue was $16.8 billion, up 45% from the prior quarter, with adjusted profitability, as it eyes an IPO.

stories.headline: Roadster, day three: how Tesla pulled off the stunts, and the 2018 tweet that called it
stories.why_read: You retweeted Hagerty's behind-the-scenes, the weight comparison, and Musk's eight-year-old thruster promise. It's the fun story you keep coming back to.
body: Hagerty's Henry Catchpole got an exclusive look behind the scenes with Tesla VP of Vehicle Engineering Lars Moravy, who walks through how the flying, kick-flipping, ceiling-sticking Roadster actually did it. Nic Cruz Patane, in another post you retweeted, says the new Roadster will be lighter than a base Model 3 RWD despite roughly 5.5 times the horsepower. You also retweeted Musk's June 2018 promise that a SpaceX option package would add about 10 small rocket thrusters that 'maybe will even allow a Tesla to fly,' plus his line this week that 'since fate maximizes for ironic entertainment,' the Roadster was always going to be a flying car.

Not everyone was charmed. X News reports flying-car startup Alef answered with video of its Model A taking off vertically and flying over a Roadster on its 1,000th flight, and MKBHD's critique of the thruster stunts and 2028 timeline set off a creator debate. A post you bookmarked from someone who studied theoretical math offered the best defense: Leibniz's binary arithmetic looked like a useless gag in 1703, and it now runs the world.

stories.headline: François Chollet: agents write nearly all the code, yet engineers work harder and the bottom line isn't moving
stories.why_read: You bookmarked this. It's a systems-thinking take that fits your DevOps lens perfectly: automate one stage and the bottleneck just moves.
body: Chollet lists four observations about the 'total' automation of software engineering: there are more software engineers now than in 2025 and demand is growing; they have never worked harder; they largely don't write code anymore, since agents write about 100% of it; and the bottom line of the companies employing them is typically not budging from AI adoption.

His conclusion: think in systems. Automating one part of a system creates its own friction and moves the bottleneck somewhere else. It pairs neatly with Anthropic's own report this week that human attention, not code generation, is now the limit.

stories.headline: Build your own PR-review agent instead of buying one, argues @CraigBarrDev
stories.why_read: You retweeted this. It's a concrete recipe a platform team could stand up on GitHub webhooks this week.
body: @CraigBarrDev's take: for the best balance of cost and quality, skip the SaaS Codex and Claude reviewers. Instead, build your own agent triggered by GitHub webhooks when a PR is opened or updated, give it company and architecture context the SaaS tools never see, and give it risk guidelines that separate nitpicks from issues that should block a merge. The agent approves or requests changes on the PR, so coding agents must address real risks before anything gets through. The underlying model can still be Codex or Claude, just not through the hosted review service.

He warns that a nitpicking agentic reviewer can be worse than none, but says the off-the-shelf tools aren't bad, 'just not great, yet.' He was replying to Boris Cherny, who says Claude Code Review runs on all his PRs and catches almost every bug before it goes in.

stories.headline: Lean now ships with verified kernels, including one Claude wrote in Lean and proved consistent
stories.why_read: Mathematics, formal proof, and AI in one release. It's a striking example of AI being used to make software provably more trustworthy.
body: Leonardo de Moura writes that AI agents have become very good at finding bugs in Lean's proof-checking kernel, so Lean v4.35.0 adds a lake check command that exports your development and rechecks it with the bare official kernel in a sandbox. Lean also now ships four more kernels, and lake check --paranoid runs them all plus a hardened-allocator build of the official one. The headline is con-leche, the first Lean kernel written in Lean and proven consistent, implemented and proven by Claude (Fable and Opus) under heavy supervision from Joachim Breitner at the Lean FRO. It checks all of Mathlib in about 100 seconds on eight threads.

To guard against compiler and runtime bugs, Breitner had AI translate con-leche to Rust, then used the Aeneas tool to prove the Rust version, con-ron, refines the original. De Moura says scale is the next problem: Anthropic's FLT project is over 13 million lines, Mathlib is 2.5 million, and proposals for billion-line math libraries are appearing.

stories.headline: Google open-sources Harness², a framework that lets agents rewrite their own prompts, tools, and memory per task
stories.why_read: Agent infrastructure from Google again, a day after AX. Self-tuning harnesses are the kind of thing your bot fleet could use directly.
body: X News reports Harness² is a plug-and-play framework that lets AI agents recursively refine their execution setup, including prompts, tools, and memory, for each new task. It works through propose, probe, and compose steps and builds a library of lessons for later tasks.

On benchmarks like WorkBuddy-Bench it lifted scores by up to 11.5 points in a single step, with bigger gains over multiple rounds in tests with GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash. The code is available under Apache 2.0.

stories.headline: OpenAI 'Aurora' model names flash briefly in the API
stories.why_read: An early tea-leaf for the next frontier release. Treat it as a sighting, not a launch.
body: X News reports that model names tagged 'aurora' appeared in OpenAI's API, created minutes apart under OpenAI's 'system' owner tag. Testers got errors when they tried them, a 503 for the red variant and 404s for green and blue, so there's no public access, and the alpha tags plus quick removal point to internal testing.
The sighting fueled talk of a fast response to Anthropic's rumored Fable 5.5, and some linked the name to an earlier coding-focused model. OpenAI hasn't said anything officially.

stories.headline: Anthropic pitches lawmakers a narrow draft bill for frontier AI safety
stories.why_read: The lab is writing its own rulebook proposal. Worth knowing what 'narrow' means before it shows up in Congress.
body: X News reports the draft would let the government block a frontier model's release only for foreseeable risks of more than $1 billion in damages or more than 50 deaths from bioweapons, model escapes, or cyberattacks, mirroring California's recent law. Independent evaluators would check models and report urgent risks to the Commerce Department, which alone could seek a court suspension.

Reactions split: critics say it permits too much harm before anyone can step in and favors big labs, while Anthropic calls it sensible policy drawn from its safety framework. No lawmaker has introduced it yet.

stories.headline: Grok Bot users are handing it shopping, bill negotiation, and even video-editing builds
stories.why_read: Grok agents are one of your core beats, and this is the real-world usage roundup rather than the benchmark one.
body: X News rounds up user reports of Grok Bot ordering a silent basketball at the best price with free shipping, landing a 300 Mbps internet plan for $70.90 with no contract, and building a custom video editor that let one filmmaker drop Adobe Premiere. Musk highlighted a daily batch of about 20 improvements, including faster tasks, new connectors like Robinhood, and smoother voice memory, as the app climbs the Productivity charts.
Prebuilt bots for research or trading and shared custom prompts are spreading, though some users still prefer to check payments by hand.

stories.headline: Vercel Labs ports TypeScript's compiler back to TypeScript and claims it beats the Go rewrite by 2 to 4x
stories.why_read: You bookmarked this. It's a delightfully contrarian compiler story: the Go port was supposed to be the fast one.
body: Chris Tate of Vercel Labs announced tsc-ts. The story in his words: TypeScript was written in TypeScript, then rewritten in Go; Vercel Labs ported it back to TypeScript, compiled it with scriptc, and says the result is 2 to 4 times faster than tsgo.
If those numbers hold up outside Vercel's own benchmarks, it's a strong argument that ahead-of-time compilation of TypeScript itself can rival a native rewrite.

stories.headline: A 15-year sensor-fusion veteran argues fusion is a crutch and only vision sees meaning
stories.why_read: You bookmarked this video. It's the engineering version of the camera-only argument behind the Robotaxis you watch in Austin.
body: @nymbusjp, who says he spent 15 years building multi-sensor fusion systems, walks through why he now thinks fusion is a crutch: more sensors don't mean more information, and lidar and radar have physical limits in rain, with blooming, and in how well they can separate targets on a range-Doppler grid.
His argument is that only vision captures meaning, which lines up with Tesla's camera-only bet.

stories.headline: A record 12,700 US-based tech professionals moved back to India in the first nine months of 2026
stories.why_read: You retweeted this one. It's the reverse of the path you took, and it says a lot about where tech talent thinks the opportunity is now.
body: Indian Tech & Infra reports that a record 12,700 US-based tech professionals returned to India in the first nine months of 2026. The post drew more than 15,000 likes.

The post itself is one line and an image, with no breakdown of reasons, but the number lands in the same week as Anthropic's report on shrinking junior technical hiring and a running debate about where AI-era engineering jobs will be.

stories.headline: A Model Y owner says his car tried to dodge a truck hitting it from behind at 50 mph
stories.why_read: You retweeted this. A small, human story about safety tech doing its job, and the driver walked away.
body: @BillyKryzak writes that he was sitting at a light in his Model Y when a large truck rear-ended him at about 50 mph. He says the car tried to get out of the way on its own, driving forward and turning, which kept it from slamming into the car ahead and lessened the impact.
He reports zero injuries and says he'll replace the car with another Tesla. 'The car actively tried to save me,' he wrote.

stories.headline: US home sellers outnumber buyers by more than 580,000, the widest gap on record
stories.why_read: You retweeted this. Useful context for anyone watching home prices around Austin.
body: Charlie Bilello reports that US home sellers are now estimated to outnumber homebuyers by over 580,000, or 63%, the largest gap in data going back to 2013.
A market with that many more sellers than buyers usually means more negotiating leverage for buyers and pressure on asking prices.

stories.headline: The EU moves to fast-track Project Bromo, a €6.5 billion satellite venture meant to rival Starlink
stories.why_read: Europe's answer to the SpaceX constellation you follow. The hard part, as skeptics note, is launch cost.
body: X News reports the European Union plans to quickly approve Project Bromo, a joint venture merging the satellite manufacturing businesses of Airbus, Leonardo, and Thales into a €6.5 billion company aimed at rivaling SpaceX. The push follows concerns about dependence on Starlink after disruptions in Ukraine and US restrictions on military use.
Supporters, including Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, back building industrial champions, while skeptics point to higher launch costs, job disputes, and the need for heavy subsidies.

stories.headline: Neuralink says its first Blindsight vision implants could come within 6 to 12 months
stories.why_read: Science with a big human payoff: restoring sight even to people blind from birth.
body: X News reports Neuralink aims to implant its first vision-restoring Blindsight devices in the next six to 12 months. The system skips the eyes and optic nerve entirely, using a camera to capture the scene and wirelessly writing signals straight to the visual cortex, which in principle works even for people blind since birth. It has had FDA Breakthrough Device Designation since 2024.
Longer term, the company talks about sharper-than-normal vision and extra senses like infrared and radar, and it's also working on restoring full-body movement.

stories.headline: Musk opens Walter Isaacson's new podcast series on AI, robots, and his DOGE regrets
stories.why_read: A long-form conversation from the biographer who knows him best, out Tuesday.
body: X News reports the episode premieres October 20 as the first in Isaacson's new series of in-depth conversations with tech leaders, including Peter Thiel and Fei-Fei Li, produced by Kaleidoscope and distributed by iHeart.

Musk argues the national debt will take AI and robots to solve, not just spending cuts, and admits he got too involved in the Department of Government Efficiency, which kept him from his companies longer than planned. He also talks up Starship, Starlink, Neuralink, and self-driving, and predicts AI will surpass humans within five years.

stories.headline: Show HN: Sphinx is a Git hook that quizzes you on your agent's code before it lets you push
stories.why_read: 'Outsource your thinking, not your understanding.' A clever guardrail for anyone shipping agent-written code at scale.
body: Sphinx is a free, open-source Git hook. When you or your agent push to a protected branch, a reviewer model that never saw your chat reads the diff and asks what the change does when things go wrong. Answer wrong and it explains why and tries a new scenario; answer right and the push continues. It works with Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, Pi, or plain Git, and can run on your existing agent, OpenRouter, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
Your answers never reach the coding agent, and it never opens .env files or keys. In a hurry, 'sphinx yolo' lets a push through but logs every skip.

stories.headline: Pele renders Mermaid diagrams to themeable SVG up to 500 times faster than Mermaid.js
stories.why_read: You build a lot of diagrams. This is a zero-dependency renderer that themes with plain CSS variables.
body: Pele is a lightweight open-source library that takes Mermaid syntax and renders SVG, themed with CSS variables so color changes apply without re-rendering. Its site claims zero dependencies, a 230 kB gzipped bundle versus 1.6 MB for Mermaid.js, and render times of 0.05 to 0.3 ms versus 6 to 82 ms.
It supports every diagram type built into Mermaid 12.1.0 and adapts layouts for small screens. It was developed for Obsidian, to render diagrams quickly and match your theme.

stories.headline: Show HN: llmspeed lets you feel how fast a local model will run before you buy the hardware
stories.why_read: Before you buy that M5 Ultra or RTX 5090 for your local models, try this. It covers DeepSeek V4.1 Flash too.
body: llmspeed simulates the token speed of local models on specific hardware, from an RTX 3060 to an RTX PRO 6000, AMD Strix Halo, DGX Spark, and Mac Studio M5 Ultra, across models such as Qwen 3.8, GLM-5.3, Gemma 4, GPT-OSS, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.

Measured numbers come from community benchmarks such as r/LocalLLaMA and localscore.ai, and the rest are derived from similar setups or projected from specs. The code and data are open source on GitHub.

stories.headline: Bleached corals recover within days when they touch a healthy neighbor
stories.why_read: A hopeful, kind-hearted science story for a Sunday, and one of the top Hacker News posts.
body: Nature reports that researchers restored bleached coral in a lab by putting it in contact with a healthy fragment. The two form a tissue bridge, and the healthy fragment passes along the symbiotic algae the bleached coral lost, reversing the bleaching in days. The findings were published in Science Advances on October 14.

It started by accident: in early 2025 Stephen Palumbi at Hopkins Marine Station noticed color seeping into a bleached branch where two fragments were touching. PhD student Danny Collins then tested pairs of fragments from the same Pocillopora damicornis coral. Stanford's Fiorenza Micheli called the result 'incredible' and said it may inspire scalable solutions.

stories.headline: Making chicken transparent with the dye in Dorito dust
stories.why_read: Physics and chemistry you can try in a kitchen, written with a lot of humor.
body: A hobbyist physicist tried to replicate part of a paper, 'Achieving optical transparency in live animals with absorbing molecules,' by soaking raw chicken breast in tartrazine, the bright yellow-orange dye found on Doritos. A 2 mm slice soaked for six hours in about 0.19 M solution became partly see-through, with a grid visible underneath and a gummy-bear look. The paper used 0.62 M at 40 °C on a shaker, which the author couldn't do safely at home.

The working explanation: the dye's absorption shifts the refractive index of water toward that of proteins and lipids, so light scatters less and the tissue turns clearer. A more ambitious replication is coming.

stories.headline: antirez's Commodore 64 simulator lets you lift a chip's leg and watch the machine break
stories.why_read: Close to the metal in the most literal sense, from the creator of Redis.
body: c64-hw-sim simulates the Commodore 64 motherboard, board ASSY 250407, pin by pin. You can lift a chip's leg, short it to ground or +5V, pull a chip from its socket, or open a resistor, then watch the screen, keyboard, and every signal on the board. It knows only the netlist and each chip's pin behavior, so any garbage on screen is computed from the circuit, not scripted.

One example: lift pin 17 of the color RAM before power-on and the machine looks healthy because reads and writes alias the same way; put it back and the unwritten half shows up as random colors. antirez pitches it for learning and for diagnosing real broken boards so you desolder as few chips as possible.
